title: DNS Systems: Name Resolution
subject: DNS Architecture
description: The 'Phonebook of the Internet' is broken. Resolve complex resolution failures, service record gaps, and cache poisoning symptoms using forensic evidence.
reportOverview: This module tests deep DNS logic. Key skills: SRV record registration for Active Directory, CNAME vs A-record efficiency, Scavenging/Aging mechanics, and Root Hint failover.
evidenceInstructions:
Instructions:
1) Analyze the 'Artifact' for Red Herrings (clues that look relevant but aren't).
2) Use Triage to narrow the scope.
3) Diagnose the architectural failure.
4) Review the Resolution Insight for the 'Professional Standard' fix.

tickets.title: "Intranet is down, but only for some people"
tickets.summary: The 'Portal' site moved to a new IP. Half the staff sees the new site, the other half gets a '404' or the old site.
artifact: Red Herring: Web server CPU is at 10%

triage.q: What happens when a name has two different 'A' records pointing to different IPs?
options: DNS uses 'Round Robin' to alternate between them

diagnosis.q: Why is the old IP still in the system?
options: Scavenging is disabled, so the 'stale' record wasn't removed when the server moved

fix.q: How do you ensure this doesn't happen again?
options: Delete old record and enable Scavenging/Aging

debrief.summary: DNS is only as good as its maintenance.
debrief.takeaway: Resolution Insight: You caught the 'Ghost' record. Without Scavenging, DNS is a phonebook that never crosses out people who move away. By enabling Scavenging, the server now 'audits' itself to ensure every record is still valid.

tickets.title: "Domain logins are failing with 'No DC Found'"
tickets.summary: Computers can ping the Domain Controller's IP, but they cannot join the domain or log users in.
artifact: Red Herring: The 'Workstation' service is running

triage.q: Which record type is the 'GPS' that tells a PC where the Domain Controller service is located?

diagnosis.q: Why is the computer unable to find the DC despite a successful ping?
options: The Service (SRV) records are missing from DNS

fix.q: How do you force the DC to re-register its 'GPS' coordinates?
options: Restart the 'Netlogon' service on the DC

debrief.summary: Active Directory relies entirely on SRV records to function.
debrief.takeaway: Resolution Insight: You realized that 'knowing the server is there' (IP) isn't the same as 'knowing what the server does' (Service). Restarting Netlogon forces the DC to write its resume back into DNS so clients can find it.

tickets.title: "External sites load slow, then fail"
tickets.summary: Browsing Google or Microsoft works for 10 minutes after a server reboot, then stops completely.
artifact: Red Herring: ISP Gateway is pingable

triage.q: If your Forwarders (8.8.8.8) stop responding, what is the 'backup' method for internet resolution?

diagnosis.q: Why is resolution failing completely when the forwarder is sluggish?
options: The server isn't allowed to 'ask the 13 masters' (Root Hints) for help
Enable 'Use root hints if no forwarders are available'

debrief.summary: Root Hints are the 'Safety Net' of the global internet.
debrief.takeaway: Resolution Insight: Forwarders are like calling a smart friend. Root Hints are like going to the library yourself. By enabling Root Hints, you ensured that even if Google's DNS is down, your server can still find its own way around the web.

tickets.title: "I need the name of the PC at 10.0.0.45"
tickets.summary: The Firewall shows an attack from 10.0.0.45. You need to identify the machine name immediately.
artifact: Red Herring: The Forward Lookup Zone is healthy

triage.q: Which zone type is responsible for 'Reverse' lookups (IP to Name)?

options: The Reverse Lookup Zone hasn't been created for this subnet
Create a Reverse Lookup Zone (PTR records)

debrief.summary: Reverse Lookups are 'Caller ID' for the network.
debrief.takeaway: Resolution Insight: Most DNS is set up to find names. Security requires the opposite. By creating the Reverse Zone, you enabled the server to provide 'Caller ID,' allowing you to track down the infected device by its IP.

tickets.title: "The 'Shop' link breaks whenever we change servers"
tickets.summary: Marketing uses 'shop.local'. Every time you upgrade the web server hardware (new IP), you have to update 5 different records and 200 bookmarks break.
artifact: Current Setup: 5 A-records for 'shop' pointing to .50
Red Herring: The server is a Virtual Machine

triage.q: What record type acts as a 'nickname' for another name?

diagnosis.q: Why is the current setup inefficient?
options: It's hard to manage multiple A-records for one service
Create one A-record for the server, then CNAMEs for the services

debrief.summary: CNAMEs abstract the service from the hardware.
debrief.takeaway: Resolution Insight: You decoupled the 'service' from the 'server.' Now, if the hardware changes, you update one single A-record, and the CNAME 'nickname' automatically points to the new location without marketing changing a thing.

tickets.title: "Secondary server isn't getting updates"
tickets.summary: You added a record to DC-01. DC-02 doesn't see it, even after 'Reload'.
artifact: Red Herring: Ping between DCs is 1ms

triage.q: What process syncs the DNS database between two servers?

diagnosis.q: Why is DC-02 out of sync?
options: DC-01 hasn't 'allowed' zone transfers to DC-02's IP

debrief.summary: DNS sync is a security-gated process.
debrief.takeaway: Resolution Insight: DNS servers don't just give their data to anyone who asks. You had to 'whitelist' the secondary server to allow it to pull the records, ensuring consistency across the office.

tickets.title: "I fixed the IP, but it's still pinging the old one"
tickets.summary: You updated the record on the server. The user's PC still goes to the wrong IP.
artifact: Red Herring: The user rebooted their router

triage.q: Where does a PC store DNS answers locally to save time?

diagnosis.q: Why is the PC ignoring the server's update?
options: The PC is using its 'cached' memory of the old answer

fix.q: How do you empty the PC's memory?

debrief.summary: The local cache can lead to 'stale' behavior on the client.
debrief.takeaway: Resolution Insight: Speed can be a downside. The PC was trying to be fast by not asking the server. Flushing the cache forces it to see the 'new truth' you created on the DNS server.

tickets.title: "External mail is bouncing with 'Domain not found'"
tickets.summary: We can send emails to clients, but when they reply, they get an error saying our domain doesn't exist.
artifact: Public DNS: A-record for mail exists

triage.q: Which record type identifies the 'Mail Server' for a domain?

diagnosis.q: Why is the internet rejecting the mail?
options: There is no 'Post Office' sign (MX record) telling the internet where to drop the mail
Add an MX record pointing to your mail server's A-record

debrief.summary: MX records are essential for global mail routing.
debrief.takeaway: Resolution Insight: An A-record tells the world 'I exist.' An MX record tells the world 'Send my mail here.' Without the MX record, other mail servers simply didn't know which of your servers was the 'official' receiver.

tickets.title: "Resolution is slow for only one specific website"
tickets.summary: Everything is fast except for 'partner-portal.com', which takes 30 seconds to load every time.
artifact: Specific Setting: A 'Conditional Forwarder' exists for 'partner-portal.com' pointing to an old IP

triage.q: If a server has a 'Conditional Forwarder' and a 'General Forwarder', which does it use first?

diagnosis.q: Why is the load time so high?
options: It's trying the dead IP in the Conditional Forwarder first, timing out, then falling back
Delete or update the Conditional Forwarder

debrief.summary: Specific rules always override general rules in DNS.
debrief.takeaway: Resolution Insight: You found a 'forgotten' rule. Because you told the server to 'always ask THIS specific IP' for that partner site, it was dutifully waiting for a response that never came before trying the regular internet.

tickets.title: "DNS Service won't start - Error 2"
tickets.summary: After a power outage, the DNS role stays stopped. Attempting to start it results in a 'File not found' error.
artifact: Red Herring: Registry shows the service is enabled

triage.q: Where does a non-Active Directory integrated zone store its data?

diagnosis.q: Why is the service failing to start?
options: The physical zone files are missing or corrupted
Restore .dns files from backup to the DNS folder

debrief.summary: Standard DNS zones are just text files on the disk.
debrief.takeaway: Resolution Insight: You went 'under the hood.' If the zone isn't in Active Directory, it's just a file. If that file is gone, the 'brain' of the DNS server is empty. Restoring the file from backup restores the entire configuration.
